article.overview: A mineralogical mapping instrument is a remote-sensing spectrometer or multiband imager that identifies the minerals present on a planetary surface from the way that surface reflects sunlight at different wavelengths. On the Moon, such instruments are normally flown on orbiters, where they map which rock types and minerals occur across large areas, supporting studies of crustal history and of lunar mineral resources. Instruments in this class differ widely in wavelength coverage, spectral sampling, spatial resolution, mass and power, so each specification must be tied to a named instrument.
article.description:
A mineralogical mapping instrument records sunlight reflected from the lunar surface in many narrow wavelength bands. Minerals absorb light at characteristic wavelengths, so measuring these absorption features across a scene allows the instrument to infer which minerals are present and how they are distributed. Clementine's filters were chosen to show absorption bands diagnostic of iron-bearing minerals [6], and hydroxyl and water features occur near 3000 nm [1].

Most lunar mineral mappers are carried on orbiters and observe the surface from tens to hundreds of kilometres. Their spatial resolution is set by altitude, optics and detector. Some instruments record hundreds of contiguous spectral channels (an imaging spectrometer), while others use a handful of filters in front of area detectors (a multiband imager or camera). The examples in this article span both designs, so they should not be read as one standard instrument.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The purpose of a lunar mineralogical mapping instrument is to determine what the Moon's surface is made of and how that composition varies between geological units. The Moon Mineralogy Mapper's stated primary science goal was to characterise and map lunar surface mineralogy in the context of lunar geologic evolution, covering the highland crust, basaltic volcanism, impact craters and potential volatiles [1]. Its exploration goal was to assess and map lunar mineral resources at high spatial resolution to support future targeted missions [1].

Applications follow from these objectives: mapping rock types exposed in crater walls and basin ejecta, comparing mare basalts with highland material, locating hydroxyl- or water-bearing features, and providing compositional context for future mission planning. These applications reflect the stated objectives of the cited instruments and are not all demonstrated in every mission.
article.operating_principle:
Lunar mineral mappers normally measure solar radiation reflected from the surface, so they operate in daylight. The M3 is described as a pushbroom imaging spectrometer that measures solar-reflected energy with a two-dimensional HgCdTe detector array [1]. The Clementine UV-VIS camera instead used a six-position filter wheel in front of a CCD framing imager, and its NIR camera used a separate CCD imager with six filters [6]. The SELENE Multiband Imager used bandpass filters with two-dimensional detectors, and the Spectral Profiler used a diffraction grating [5].

For each pixel, the measured reflectance across the wavelength bands is compared with calibrated reference spectra, or with the position and depth of absorption features, to infer mineral signatures. Calibration against solar irradiance and in-flight reference targets is essential, because raw signal levels are not directly mineral information.
article.scientific_importance: Remote mineralogical mapping is one of the few ways to observe the composition of large areas of the Moon's surface in a systematic way. The Clementine mission produced multispectral image data that its authors describe as the first global digital data set of the Moon [6]. Later instruments extended spectral coverage into the near-infrared: the Moon Mineralogy Mapper was specified to cover about 0.7 to 3.0 micrometres, which includes the diagnostic absorptions of the main lunar minerals and the fundamental hydroxyl and water absorptions near 3000 nm [1], and the Chandrayaan-2 Imaging Infrared Spectrometer is specified to cover 0.8 to 5.0 micrometres [4]. Maps derived from such data can show the distribution of rock types, the composition of volcanic deposits and water-related features. Interpretation remains limited by spatial resolution, calibration, illumination geometry and the need for laboratory and sample data to confirm mineral identifications.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a mineralogical mapping instrument. The four examples below are historical or orbital designs with documented values in the sources reviewed for this article. Values are tied to each named instrument and are not generalised across the class.

examples.name: Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3), Chandrayaan-1
examples.type: Flown imaging spectrometer (guest instrument on ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter)
examples.spatial_resolution_m_per_pixel: 70 (from 100 km orbit; 140 m in 2x2-averaged Global mode)
examples.field_of_view: 40 km across track from 100 km orbit (ISSDC); 24 degrees (JPL characterisation); both reported, not reconciled
examples.detector: Two-dimensional HgCdTe detector array (ISSDC); multi-stage passive cooler for detector and spectrometer (JPL)
examples.construction_note: Built by JPL; Brown University named as a partner institution (ISSDC payload summary).
examples.qualification: Mass and power values come from a JPL early-assessment abstract (8 kg, 15 W, volume 25x18x12 cm) and the ISSDC payload summary (8.2 kg). These differ and are reported as given. The JPL abstract describes the in-flight performance as consistent with laboratory values but does not give a formal qualification report. Mission end date not verified in this run.

examples.name: Imaging Infrared Spectrometer (IIRS), Chandrayaan-2
examples.type: Flown hyperspectral imager (instrument on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter)
examples.spectral_resolution_nm: approximately 20 to 25 (ISRO instrument description); approximately 20 (ISRO objectives)
examples.swath: not stated in the ISRO page reviewed
examples.qualification: The ISRO page describes IIRS as a hyperspectral optical imaging instrument that maps lunar geomorphology and mineralogy. Mass, power and swath are not publicly specified in the sources checked in this run. The ISRO page links a payload handbook that was not retrieved. Operational status and data release were not verified in this run.

examples.name: SELENE (Kaguya) LISM: Multiband Imager (MI) and Spectral Profiler (SP)
examples.type: Flown orbital imaging and spectroscopy instruments (SELENE / Kaguya orbiter, JAXA)
examples.mi_bands: 9 in total: visible 0.415, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95 and 1.0 micrometres; near-infrared 1.0, 1.05, 1.25 and 1.55 micrometres; band widths 10 to 50 nm
examples.mi_spatial_resolution_m: visible 20; near-infrared 62 (as tabulated on the JAXA page; altitude basis not stated in the extracted table)
examples.mi_optics: Two nadir-looking telescopes with two-dimensional detectors and bandpass filters
examples.sp_spectral_range_um: visible 0.52 to 0.96; near-infrared 0.9 to 1.7 and 1.7 to 2.6
examples.sp_spatial_resolution_m: 562 x 400 (as printed on the JAXA page; table is partly garbled)
examples.sp_optics: Diffraction grating; observes the lunar surface below the spacecraft
examples.qualification: The JAXA LISM page is an older, mission-era description. Mass, power and dimensions are not given on the page reviewed. Spectral and spatial values are as published there and were not checked against a later calibration or data-release document.

examples.name: Clementine UV-VIS and near-infrared (NIR) cameras
examples.type: Flown multispectral imaging cameras (Clementine spacecraft, 1994 lunar mission)
examples.uvvis_detector: CCD framing imager with a six-position filter wheel
examples.nir_detector: Near-infrared CCD imager with six filters
examples.qualification: The NASA technical memorandum describes the two cameras as an 11-channel imaging spectrometer for surface composition. The 140 kg figure is the spacecraft mass, not the camera mass. Camera mass and power are not given in the text reviewed. The memorandum notes that spatial resolution varied because of the elliptical orbit.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Documented dimensions exist only for the M3 (a stated volume of 25 x 18 x 12 cm in the JPL abstract [2]) and are not given for the IIRS, the Kaguya LISM instruments or the Clementine cameras in the sources reviewed. Because the designs differ in optics, detector format and wavelength coverage, their envelopes are not comparable. An instrument's dimensions must be set from its optical design, thermal and mounting requirements, and the spacecraft's accommodation envelope.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Documented masses are 8.2 kg (or 8 kg) for the M3 [1][2]. Masses for the IIRS, the Kaguya LISM instruments and the Clementine cameras were not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The Clementine 140 kg figure is the spacecraft mass and must not be read as an instrument mass [6]. Mass affects launch accommodation and must be taken from the flight-configuration source for each instrument.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The M3 is given as about 15 W [2]. Power for the IIRS, the Kaguya LISM instruments and the Clementine cameras was not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Detector cooling and thermal control add to the power budget where a cooler is used, as in the M3 [2].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A mineralogical mapping instrument flies on an orbiting spacecraft and depends on sunlight, so measurements are normally made in daylight and depend on illumination geometry. The M3 detector and spectrometer were cooled by a multi-stage passive cooler [2]. The Clementine sensors were noted to degrade in the deep-space, hard-radiation environment [6]. The M3 early assessment also reported scattered light from its lightweight diamond-turned mirrors affecting the visible part of the spectrum [2]. Orbit altitude and optics set the footprint size: the M3 gives about 70 m per pixel from a 100 km orbit [1], and the Clementine average resolution was about 200 m per pixel, varying with the spacecraft's elliptical orbit [6]. Operating temperature limits, radiation tolerance and survival requirements are not publicly specified for the examples in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: Reflectance spectroscopy from orbit senses the illuminated surface only, depends on illumination and viewing geometry and needs calibration before mineral identifications are made. Spatial resolution depends on altitude and mode: M3 Target mode gives 70 m per pixel from a 100 km orbit and its Global mode gives 140 m [1][2]. Sources for the M3 disagree on some parameters, and the Kaguya page is an older description with a partly garbled table. The examples do not share one specification, so values must not be combined across instruments.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All four examples are orbital instruments. Their transportation chain is spacecraft integration, launch, transfer, lunar orbit insertion, commissioning and operations rather than surface delivery. No surface deployment, rover stowage or sample handling applies.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with the orbiter's payload accommodation on Earth. For the Moon Mineralogy Mapper this was a guest-instrument integration onto ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft [1][2].
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle. Chandrayaan-1 launched on 22 October 2008 [2]; Clementine was launched on a Titan II booster from Vandenberg [6].
Transfer to the Moon. Clementine reached lunar orbit through two highly eccentric phasing orbits before its lunar insertion burn [6].
Commission the instrument in orbit. M3 acquired its first imaging data on 18 and 19 November 2008 in Target and Global modes, with further commissioning data on 22 and 24 November 2008 [2].
Operate the instrument under the spacecraft's pointing, thermal and data-handling control, with the detector temperature held near its nominal value [2].
Calibrate and validate the in-flight performance against reference observations; JPL reported that calibration validation was planned to continue beyond commissioning [2].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The instruments are fixed to orbiting spacecraft and do not deploy on the surface. Operation depends on spacecraft pointing, detector thermal conditions and in-flight calibration. The M3 detector and spectrometer were cooled by a multi-stage passive cooler [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: M3 flew as a guest instrument on Chandrayaan-1 [1][2]. IIRS is carried on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [4]. The SELENE (Kaguya) LISM suite was flown on the Kaguya orbiter [5]. The Clementine UV-VIS and NIR cameras flew on the Clementine spacecraft in 1994 [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not applicable to a lander or rover, and no lander compatibility is claimed. These were orbiter payloads. A new mineralogical mapper would need its own interface assessment against the orbiter's pointing, thermal, power and data systems; no specific spacecraft interface was verified for this article.

article.historical_significance: Clementine (1994) produced multispectral image data that its authors describe as the first global digital data set of the Moon, and it used filters chosen to show absorption bands diagnostic of iron-bearing minerals [6]. The Moon Mineralogy Mapper was a NASA guest instrument on ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 mission; its early in-flight assessment reported that its measurements were consistent with laboratory-measured spectral, radiometric, spatial and uniformity characteristics [2]. The Indian IIRS on Chandrayaan-2 was designed to study minerals, water and hydroxyl, with an objective to characterise the hydroxyl/water feature near 3.0 micrometres [4]. The SELENE LISM suite on the Kaguya orbiter had the stated aim of providing precise topographic, geologic and mineralogical information of the Moon [5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name 'mineralogical mapping instrument' describes a class of remote-sensing instruments rather than one standard design. The four examples in this article were built for different missions and are not interchangeable. Values such as mass, power, spectral range and resolution must always be read against the named instrument and its source. Two sources disagree for the Moon Mineralogy Mapper (mass, spectral range and field of view), and no mass or power values were found for some examples. The generic environmental and deployment discussion describes engineering considerations; it is not a certified design specification for a new instrument.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Moon Mineralogy Mapper sources disagree: mass 8.2 kg (ISSDC) versus 8 kg (JPL abstract); spectral range 0.7 to 3.0 micrometres (ISSDC) versus 406 to 2991 nm (JPL Target-mode table); field of view 40 km (ISSDC) versus 24 degrees (JPL). Both are reported as published; the JPL abstract is an early-assessment document.

No photograph of the M3, IIRS or Clementine camera hardware was verified. The only verified M3 image is a NASA data composite of the Orientale Basin, which is placed in the overview and is not a picture of the instrument.

The two SELENE LISM photographs (img_sp_001.jpg and img_tc_003.jpg) are labelled by the JAXA equipment page as the SP and MI flight models respectively. The identity of the hardware was not independently confirmed, and the 'tc' prefix on the MI image may indicate a labelling inconsistency. Credit and reuse conditions are not stated.

Kaguya LISM spatial-resolution and spectral values come from an older JAXA page whose specification table is partly garbled; the spatial figure 562 x 400 m was reported as printed and not checked against a calibration document. The 20 m and 62 m MI resolutions are reported as tabulated, and the altitude basis was not stated.

Mass, power, dimensions and operating status are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for the IIRS, the Kaguya LISM instruments and the Clementine cameras. The ISRO IIRS payload handbook was linked but not retrieved.

IIRS swath was not stated in the ISRO page reviewed, and the statement that IIRS is on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter comes from a search-result payload listing rather than the ISRO page. The IIRS band count is given as about 250 (ISRO page); a separate 2021 Current Science paper was located in search results but was not read, so it is not cited.

The Clementine 140 kg value is spacecraft mass and is not an instrument mass. The NTRS memorandum describes the NIR detector as a CCD imager; a secondary search summary suggested an InSb detector, which was not confirmed in the primary text and is not used.

Mission operating dates for Chandrayaan-1, Kaguya and Chandrayaan-2 (end of operations, status) were not verified against primary sources in this run. Only the Chandrayaan-1 launch and commissioning dates and the Clementine 1994 lunar-mapping period are stated, from the NTRS and JPL documents.
The 2011 JGR instrument paper on the M3 (Green et al., doi 10.1029/2011JE003797), identified in search results, was not accessed and is not cited.

Image rights: the NASA Photojournal image is a NASA-hosted product and the JAXA images are hosted by JAXA. Neither source page states public-domain status for this use; reuse should be checked against NASA media guidelines and JAXA terms before republication.
Lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is not claimed for any instrument. All four examples are orbital payloads and no surface lunar location is recommended, as deferred by the user.
The lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
